title: A Billion Friends
story: The catalog outgrew its biggest box twice this year. Vertical scaling is officially dead; replicas only multiply READ capacity, and writes still funnel into one primary.
The industry answer: split the data itself across machines. The dangerous part is WHERE each row lives — and what happens when that mapping changes.

briefing: [GRAFANA] shard-eu CPU 97% - shards us/ap idle at 20%
DM from Priya - my EU shop is slow AGAIN

checks.label: per-shard QPS dashboard
checks.out:
shard-us   1,240 qps
shard-ap   1,180 qps
shard-eu   8,900 qps

One shard carries half the fleet's load.

checks.label: SELECT country, count(*) FROM users GROUP BY 1
checks.out:
country | count
DE       | 31%
IN       | 28%
GB       | 12%
US       | 9%
...

You sharded by COUNTRY. Two countries own the majority of rows and traffic.

checks.label: simulate adding a node with hash(key) mod N
checks.out:
Adding node #4 under naive modulo remaps 71% of keys.
Every almost-key moves = mass migration + cache apocalypse.

fixes.label: Add a read replica to the hot shard, hope writes stay flat
fixes.successText: EU reads breathe for a quarter. Then EU sellers grow another 40% and you are back in this exact room.
fixes.lesson: Replicating a hot shard copies the problem; rebalancing the key space solves it.

fixes.label: Rehash onto consistent-hashed ring with virtual nodes

deepDive.title: Consistent Hashing & Virtual Nodes
deepDive.body: Place nodes on a hash ring; each key belongs to the next node clockwise. When a node joins or dies, only its ring-neighborhood moves (~1/N of keys), not everything. Virtual nodes (each physical machine appearing 100-200 times on the ring) smooth out skew so no single country can dominate a shard again. This trick powers Cassandra, DynamoDB, Discord — and your catalog now too.

fixes.successText: Keys redistribute smoothly; shard-eu drops to 2,100 qps while total cluster capacity triples. Priya's shop renders before her thumb leaves the screen.
fixes.lesson: Shard by high-cardinality keys on a consistent hash ring — and never let one customer own your hottest node.

quiz.q: Why does consistent hashing beat hash(key) mod N?
options: It hashes faster on modern CPUs
Adding/removing a node moves only ~1/N of keys instead of nearly all
It automatically replicates data three times
quiz.explain: Modulo arithmetic ties every key to the total node count, so changing N remaps virtually everything. The ring approach localizes disruption to adjacent arcs.

title: The Partition Test
story: Your first overseas region goes live. During a trans-ocean cable cut, two regions both accept orders — and reconcile DIFFERENT truths when the link returns.

The textbook triangle rears its head: under a partition you cannot have both consistency and availability. Every datastore makes this choice for you; great architects choose deliberately per workload.

scenes.prompt: Which promise does each workload get?

choices.label: Split it: strong consistency for money, eventual for carts & feeds
choices.detail: Orders stay on consensus-backed SQL. Carts move to an always-writable document store that reconciles later.

deepDive.title: PACELC in Practice
deepDive.body: CAP speaks only of partitions; PACELC adds the everyday tradeoff: Else, latency vs consistency even WITHOUT failures. Document stores choose availability everywhere — every region writable, conflicts resolved last-write-wins. Perfect for carts and activity feeds where a stale thumbnail beats an error page. Money stays put because 'eventually correct' is not a phrase finance enjoys hearing about payroll.

choices.result: During the next cable cut, carts keep filling across three regions while order processing pauses gracefully for 90 seconds instead of corrupting ledgers. Both sides survive.
choices.lesson: Polyglot persistence: give each workload the consistency contract its business actually needs — not the one your favorite database markets.

choices.label: Everything stays on strongly-consistent SQL, regions pause during cuts
choices.detail: One truth, zero surprises, occasional unavailability.
choices.result: Data is pristine. But every cable hiccup now means checkout buttons spin worldwide while the quorum elects a leader.
choices.lesson: Choosing CP everywhere trades small correctness risks for guaranteed availability incidents.

choices.label: Everything becomes eventually consistent, maximum uptime
choices.detail: Always writable! What could possibly diverge?
choices.result: Uptime soars until two regional ledgers disagree about who paid for what, and reconciliation becomes a human spreadsheet festival.
choices.lesson: Eventual consistency is a loan against tomorrow — spend it only where interest rates are kind.

quiz.q: During a network partition, CAP says a distributed system must sacrifice:
quiz.explain: Partitioned nodes can either refuse requests to stay consistent (CP) or keep serving possibly-stale data (AP). Latency tradeoffs are PACELC's 'E' — a separate axis.

title: The Bouncer's Clipboard
story: A flash sale goes live and a bot farm discovers your API forty seconds later. Legitimate merchants queue behind thousands of scripted price-scrapers.
Real clubs solve this with a clipboard at the door. Your platform has an unlocked front entrance.

briefing: [ALERT] API p99 exploded 120ms -> 4.1s during sale launch
#support - merchants: app unusable exactly at drop time

checks.label: top client IPs in nginx access log
checks.out:
awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
 18402 34.x.x.x
 17233 51.x.x.x
 16001 20.x.x.x
...
Three IPs account for more traffic than your top 50,000 real users combined.

checks.label: distribution of response codes
checks.out:
200: 61%   429: 0%   500: 19%   502: 20%

Nothing is being rejected early — junk flows all the way into Postgres before dying.

checks.label: pg_stat_activity during spike
checks.out:
214 connections: 190 are scraper-driven catalog reads.
Genuine checkout queries wait behind scrapers in the same pool.

fixes.label: Manually firewall the top 200 IPs right now
fixes.successText: The farm rotates subnets within the hour and you play whack-a-mole all evening.
fixes.lesson: Manual blocks decay in hours; policy enforced in code scales forever.

fixes.label: Deploy token-bucket rate limiter keyed by API token at the edge

deepDive.title: Token Buckets & Backpressure
deepDive.body: Each client holds a bucket of tokens refilled at a steady rate; a request spends one token, empty bucket means HTTP 429 with Retry-After. Bursts still work (that's the bucket), averages stay capped (that's the tap). Crucially, rejection happens BEFORE expensive work — databases stop paying for traffic you never wanted.

fixes.successText: Scrapers receive tidy 429s at the edge while merchant checkout sails through untouched. CPU falls 60%; the next drop feels like a normal Tuesday.
fixes.lesson: Rate limiting is not distrust of users — it is physics protection for everything standing behind the door.

quiz.q: Why reject (429) at the edge instead of letting requests through?
options: Edge servers are cheaper than app servers
Early rejection prevents junk from consuming database connections and cascading
quiz.explain: Backpressure works by shedding load BEFORE it hits expensive resources — one cheap TCP response versus a hundred-dollar database connection held hostage.

title: Live Wires
story: Merchants want live order tracking: buyer pays, kitchen sees the ticket, rider gets pinged. Today that 'real-time' is 5-second polling — and polling at scale is just self-inflicted DDoS.
Sixty thousand concurrent pollers later, you owe your app servers an apology.

scenes.prompt: How does the platform go real-time?

choices.label: WebSockets + Redis pub/sub fan-out
choices.detail: Persistent connections push events instantly; pub/sub broadcasts across your server pool.

deepDive.title: Fan-out Without Tears
deepDive.body: A socket lives on ONE server, but an order event interests subscribers connected to MANY servers. Publishing to a Redis channel lets every app server pick up the event and forward it to its own sockets. Add heartbeat pings to detect dead connections hiding behind proxies — and remember load balancers need sticky sessions or shared state, because WebSockets break the stateless-app rule politely but firmly.

choices.result: Buyer taps pay; the kitchen printer chirps in under a second. Polling load vanishes and app servers throw a small party.
choices.lesson: Push beats poll: persistent sockets plus pub/sub turn fire-hose refresh into elegant event delivery.

choices.label: Cut polling interval to one second
choices.detail: Same architecture, six times the requests. Bravely done.
choices.result: Updates arrive faster... until traffic doubles and the polling army devours every spare cycle.
choices.lesson: Scaling a wasteful pattern just buys you a bigger wasteful pattern.

choices.label: Bolt on a third-party realtime SaaS
choices.detail: Someone else's websockets, your credit card.
choices.result: It works beautifully and invoices accordingly. Vendor lock-in quietly becomes core infrastructure.
choices.lesson: Buying leverage is legitimate engineering — just read the exit clauses before the wedding.

quiz.q: Why do WebSocket deployments need pub/sub (like Redis)?
options: Any server must reach sockets held by OTHER servers
Pub/sub replaces the need for heartbeats
quiz.explain: Connections are pinned to individual servers. A channel everyone subscribes to turns 'which server holds which socket' into somebody else's bookkeeping.

title: Cache Wars II
story: Redis reads are glorious. Now the team debates WRITES: should cached data be written through to Postgres immediately, or trusted in cache and flushed lazily?
Meanwhile a hot product page expires mid-flash-sale and the database learns what a thundering herd feels like.

scenes.prompt: Pick the write strategy for cart and inventory data.

choices.label: Write-through: cache and DB update together
choices.detail: Slightly slower writes; nothing cacheable is ever lost.

deepDive.title: Through, Behind & Around
deepDive.body: WRITE-THROUGH updates cache and database synchronously — carbon-copy receipts, zero loss, higher write latency. WRITE-BACK accepts writes in cache and flushes periodically — napkin math that loses whatever the coffee spills (a Redis restart) unless you add persistence discipline. WRITE-AROUND skips the cache for cold writes entirely, keeping it full of genuinely hot reads. Choose per data type, not per fashion.

choices.result: Carts survive Redis restarts untouched; inventory counts match the ledger every audit. Writes cost 4ms more and nobody notices.
choices.lesson: For data you cannot afford to lose, write-through is boring — and boring is bulletproof.

choices.label: Write-back: blazing writes, periodic flush to DB
choices.detail: Accept the risk, harvest the speed.
choices.result: Benchmark graphs look incredible until a Redis failover eats ninety seconds of carts and support invents new swear words.
choices.lesson: Write-back trades durability for speed — a fine deal only where losing data costs less than waiting for it.

choices.label: Keep cache-aside everywhere, tune TTLs and eviction
choices.detail: No new patterns; sharpen what exists.
choices.result: Hit rate climbs to 94%. Solid, honest work — the stampede question remains unanswered, glaring, patient.
choices.lesson: Tuning beats rewriting when the fundamentals are sound; just know which dragon you left in the basement.

quiz.q: A hot key expires during peak traffic. Which mitigation helps MOST?
options: Request coalescing / locks so only ONE request rebuilds the key
quiz.explain: Stampedes happen when thousands miss simultaneously. Coalescing funnels them through a single rebuild (or serves slightly-stale values) — the herd never reaches the database.

title: The Whiteboard Gauntlet
story: An investor's technical due-diligence panel wants live numbers: 'Walk us through what 10 million daily merchants actually require.' No dashboards. Just you, a whiteboard marker, and arithmetic.
This is the opening move of every system design interview ever conducted. Master it here.

scenes.prompt: Panel question one: 10M daily active merchants, each averaging 20 page views. Roughly what average request rate must the platform serve?

choices.label: ~116K rps? No wait — do it properly: 200M reads/day ÷ 86,400s ≈ 2,300 rps average
choices.detail: Daily totals ÷ seconds in a day, then apply a peak multiplier.

deepDive.title: Fermi Estimation, Weaponized
deepDive.body: The ritual: state assumptions aloud → convert DAU to events/day → divide by 86,400 for the average → multiply 3-5x for peak (traffic is lumpy, lunchtime is real) → round aggressively to powers of ten. 1M DAU × 10 reads ≈ 10M/day ≈ ~116 rps average, ~500 rps peak. Nobody grades decimals; everybody grades whether your process is sane.

choices.result: You narrate the arithmetic step by step; a partner circles '~2,300 avg, ~10K peak' and writes 'thinks like an operator' in the margin.
choices.lesson: Back-of-envelope estimation: assumptions stated out loud, powers of ten respected, precision sacrificed proudly.

choices.label: Confidently declare 'about a million requests per second'
choices.detail: Big number, big energy, no method.
choices.result: A partner asks what the DAU assumption was. The silence has texture. You rebuild the estimate properly and salvage some credibility.
choices.lesson: An unjustified number is worse than none — it signals the absence of process.

scenes.prompt: Question two: product images average 300KB. Daily storage growth and monthly bandwidth?

choices.label: 5M uploads/day × 300KB ≈ 1.5TB/day → ~45PB/year; CDN absorbs most bandwidth
choices.detail: Storage compounds daily; bandwidth is tamed by caching layers.
choices.result: 'And that's why the CDN line item exists,' you say, tapping the earlier chapters of your own story. Panel nods.
choices.lesson: Estimation connects directly to architecture decisions — storage math funds CDN contracts.

choices.label: Start calculating on fingers, abandon halfway, pivot to vibes
choices.result: The panel smiles kindly and moves on, which somehow stings more than interruption.
choices.lesson: Practice the ritual until it survives adrenaline; estimation is a rehearsal skill.

quiz.q: 1M DAU × 10 reads each ≈ what AVERAGE read rate?
quiz.explain: 10M reads ÷ 86,400 seconds ≈ 115.7 rps. Peak multipliers take it to 400-600 rps. Memorize this dance — interviews open with it.
